original_content: Green or yellow drainage from a surgical wound is normal and expected in the first 72 hours post-operatively. No escalation is required unless drainage volume is excessive.
replacement_content: Drainage colour must be interpreted in clinical context. Serous (clear to pale yellow) or serosanguineous (pink-tinged) drainage is expected in the early post-operative period. Sanguineous (frank red blood) drainage may be normal in the first hours but requires monitoring for volume and trend. Purulent (thick, opaque yellow, green, or brown) drainage at any time point is abnormal and is a sign of infection requiring immediate physician notification. Green drainage in particular is never considered normal and should always prompt escalation.
reason: This item contains a serious clinical error. Green or opaque yellow (purulent) drainage is not normal at any post-operative stage — it is a hallmark sign of surgical site infection. Teaching new graduates that it is expected and requires no escalation could directly result in delayed treatment of infection, patient harm, or sepsis. Serous or serosanguineous drainage may be normal early on, but colour interpretation must distinguish these from purulent drainage clearly.

original_content: Document wound assessment findings only when a significant change is observed. Stable wounds do not require written documentation at every shift assessment.
replacement_content: Wound assessment must be documented at every shift assessment, regardless of whether a change has occurred. Consistent per-shift documentation establishes the baseline needed to detect subtle deterioration over time, satisfies medicolegal requirements, and ensures continuity of care across the care team. Absence of documented assessment is not equivalent to a stable wound — it is a documentation gap.
reason: This item is clinically unsafe and inconsistent with nursing documentation standards and medicolegal obligations. Per-shift wound assessment documentation is a professional and regulatory requirement in most jurisdictions. Instructing new graduates to document only on change creates dangerous gaps in the clinical record, undermines trend detection, and exposes the nurse and institution to significant liability.

original_content: Wounds can safely remain undressed for up to 24 hours after the initial dressing is removed for assessment, provided the environment is clean. This gives the wound bed air exposure and reduces moisture.
replacement_content: Dressing management must follow the surgeon's orders and facility wound care protocol. Most closed surgical wounds are covered with a primary dressing for at least 48 hours post-operatively to protect against external contamination during the re-epithelialisation phase. Prolonged dressing-free intervals are not routinely recommended and should never be initiated by nursing staff without a physician order. If a dressing requires replacement, apply a new appropriate dressing promptly. Consult the wound care team or surgeon regarding dressing-free strategies if clinically indicated.
reason: This item is clinically inaccurate and unsafe. Standard evidence-based practice recommends keeping a closed incision covered for 24–48 hours minimum. Leaving a surgical wound undressed exposes it to environmental pathogens and increases SSI risk. New graduates must not act on this guidance independently.

original_content: The classic signs are redness (erythema extending >2 cm from the wound edge), warmth, oedema, and purulent drainage. Pain disproportionate to expected recovery trajectory is also a red flag. Any two signs together warrant physician notification.
replacement_content: The classic local signs of surgical site infection are erythema (redness extending beyond the wound margin), localised warmth, oedema, and purulent drainage. Pain disproportionate to the expected recovery trajectory is also a significant red flag. The presence of ANY ONE of purulent drainage, rapidly spreading erythema, or wound dehiscence warrants immediate physician notification — do not wait for two signs to be present. When two or more signs co-exist, treat this as urgent and document the time of assessment and notification.
reason: The threshold of 'any two signs' before escalating is too high and potentially dangerous. Purulent drainage alone, or rapidly spreading erythema alone, is sufficient to warrant immediate escalation. Requiring two concurrent signs before notifying a physician could delay treatment of early or rapidly progressing SSI.
